name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MATCHING_MCQ_Q01 - Match physical quantities with their SI units

questiontext.text:
Match the electrochemical quantities in List I with their corresponding SI units in List II:

List IList II
A. Resistance (\(R\))I. \(\text{S m}^{-1}\)
B. Resistivity (\(\rho\))II. \(\Omega\text{ m}\)
C. Conductivity (\(\kappa\))III. \(\text{S m}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\)
D. Molar conductivity (\(\Lambda_m\))IV. \(\Omega\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Definitions
The quantities under consideration are electrical resistance (\(R\)), resistivity (\(\rho\)), conductivity (\(\kappa\)), and molar conductivity (\(\Lambda_m\)).

Step 2: Physical Formulas and Unit Derivations
Resistance is expressed as \(R = \rho \frac{l}{A}\), and its SI unit is ohm (\(\Omega\)).
Resistivity is defined by \(\rho = \frac{R A}{l}\), yielding the SI unit \(\Omega \times \frac{\text{m}^2}{\text{m}} = \Omega\text{ m}\).
Conductivity represents the reciprocal of resistivity, \(\kappa = \frac{1}{\rho}\), giving the SI unit \(\Omega^{-1}\text{ m}^{-1} = \text{S m}^{-1}\).
Molar conductivity is defined by \(\Lambda_m = \frac{\kappa}{c}\), where \(\kappa\) is in \(\text{S m}^{-1}\) and concentration \(c\) is in \(\text{mol m}^{-3}\), resulting in the SI unit \(\frac{\text{S m}^{-1}}{\text{mol m}^{-3}} = \text{S m}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\).

Step 3: Pairwise Matching Evaluation
Resistance corresponds to \(\Omega\).
Resistivity corresponds to \(\Omega\text{ m}\).
Conductivity corresponds to \(\text{S m}^{-1}\).
Molar conductivity corresponds to \(\text{S m}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\).

Step 4: Check and Final Conceptual Answer
The derived units fully conform to SI base and derived quantity definitions.
Final Conceptual Answer: Resistance pairs with \(\Omega\), resistivity pairs with \(\Omega\text{ m}\), conductivity pairs with \(\text{S m}^{-1}\), and molar conductivity pairs with \(\text{S m}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MATCHING_MCQ_Q02 - Match commercial batteries with their characteristics

questiontext.text:
Match the electrochemical cells/batteries in List I with their characteristic features in List II:

List IList II
A. Dry cell (Leclanché cell)I. Uses zinc-mercury amalgam and maintains a constant voltage of about \(1.35\text{ V}\)
B. Mercury cellII. Secondary cell containing lead dioxide cathode and \(38\%\) sulphuric acid
C. Lead storage batteryIII. Directly converts heat of combustion of gaseous fuels into electricity with about \(70\%\) efficiency
D. Fuel cellIV. Primary cell with a zinc container anode and carbon cathode giving about \(1.5\text{ V}\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principles of Battery Types
Primary cells cannot be recharged because the redox reaction occurs only once. Secondary batteries are rechargeable through the application of an external reverse current. Fuel cells continuously convert fuel combustion free energy into electrical energy.

Step 2: Detailed Evaluation of Each Cell
The dry cell (Leclanché cell) employs a zinc container anode and a carbon rod cathode surrounded by powdered \(\text{MnO}_2\) and carbon, furnishing a potential of approximately \(1.5\text{ V}\).
The mercury cell features a \(\text{Zn(Hg)}\) amalgam anode and a paste of \(\text{HgO}\) and carbon cathode, delivering a stable potential of nearly \(1.35\text{ V}\) throughout its operational lifetime because no ions in solution undergo net concentration change.
The lead storage battery is a secondary cell consisting of a spongy lead anode, a \(\text{PbO}_2\)-packed lead grid cathode, and \(38\%\) \(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\) electrolyte solution.
The \(\text{H}_2\text{--O}_2\) fuel cell directly transforms the combustion energy of hydrogen and oxygen into electricity with approximately \(70\%\) efficiency.

Step 3: Pairwise Matching Evaluation
Dry cell pairs with the primary cell possessing a zinc container anode and carbon cathode giving about \(1.5\text{ V}\).
Mercury cell pairs with the system using zinc-mercury amalgam and maintaining a constant voltage of about \(1.35\text{ V}\).
Lead storage battery pairs with the secondary cell containing lead dioxide cathode and \(38\%\) sulphuric acid.
Fuel cell pairs with the device directly converting heat of combustion of gaseous fuels into electricity with about \(70\%\) efficiency.

Step 4: Check and Final Conceptual Answer
The operational characteristics accurately represent the technological properties described in textbook Section 2.6 and Section 2.7.
Final Conceptual Answer: Dry cell pairs with IV, mercury cell pairs with I, lead storage battery pairs with II, and fuel cell pairs with III.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MATCHING_MCQ_Q03 - Match external opposing potential with cell behavior

questiontext.text:
For a standard Daniell cell (\(E^\circ = 1.1\text{ V}\)) with \(1\text{ M}\) \(\text{Zn}^{2+}\) and \(1\text{ M}\) \(\text{Cu}^{2+}\) solutions, match the applied opposing external potential (\(E_{\text{ext}}\)) in List I with the observed cell behavior in List II:

List IList II
A. \(E_{\text{ext}} = 0\text{ V}\)I. Reaction stops completely; no current or electron flow occurs
B. \(E_{\text{ext}} < 1.1\text{ V}\)II. Cell functions as an electrolytic cell; zinc deposits on zinc rod and copper dissolves
C. \(E_{\text{ext}} = 1.1\text{ V}\)III. Spontaneous galvanic reaction proceeds at full standard potential; electrons flow from zinc to copper
D. \(E_{\text{ext}} > 1.1\text{ V}\)IV. Galvanic cell continues to discharge; electrons flow from zinc to copper but under reduced net driving voltage

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Governing Principles of Opposing Potential
The standard Daniell cell provides an electromotive force of \(1.1\text{ V}\). When an opposing external voltage \(E_{\text{ext}}\) is connected across the electrodes, the net cell behavior depends on the magnitude of \(E_{\text{ext}}\) relative to \(1.1\text{ V}\).

Step 2: Step-by-Step Analysis of Each Condition
At \(E_{\text{ext}} = 0\text{ V}\), no opposing potential is present, so the cell operates spontaneously as a normal galvanic cell, driving electron flow from the zinc rod to the copper rod at full standard potential of \(1.1\text{ V}\).
When \(E_{\text{ext}} < 1.1\text{ V}\), the opposing voltage reduces the net electromotive force, but the cell continues to function galvanically with electrons flowing from zinc to copper and zinc dissolving at the anode.
When \(E_{\text{ext}} = 1.1\text{ V}\), the external counter-potential exactly balances the internal cell potential. No net chemical change occurs, and electrical current is zero.
When \(E_{\text{ext}} > 1.1\text{ V}\), the external voltage overcomes the cell potential and forces the reverse non-spontaneous reaction. The cell functions as an electrolytic cell, wherein electrons flow from copper to zinc, zinc deposits at the zinc electrode, and copper dissolves at the copper electrode.

Step 3: Pairwise Matching Evaluation
An external potential of \(0\text{ V}\) corresponds to spontaneous galvanic reaction at full standard potential.
An external potential less than \(1.1\text{ V}\) corresponds to continued galvanic discharge under reduced net driving voltage.
An external potential equal to \(1.1\text{ V}\) corresponds to complete cessation of chemical reaction and zero current.
An external potential exceeding \(1.1\text{ V}\) corresponds to electrolytic cell operation with zinc deposition and copper dissolution.

Step 4: Check and Final Conceptual Answer
The operational outcomes align with the principles illustrated in textbook opposing cell potential concepts.
Final Conceptual Answer: A pairs with III, B pairs with IV, C pairs with I, and D pairs with II.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MATCHING_MCQ_Q04 - Match electrode processes with electrochemical systems

questiontext.text:
Match the electrochemical system and electrode process in List I with the corresponding chemical reaction in List II:

List IList II
A. Cathode reaction in dry cellI. \(\text{O}_2(\text{g}) + 4\text{H}^+(\text{aq}) + 4\text{e}^- \rightarrow 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(\text{l})\)
B. Anode reaction in mercury cellII. \(\text{PbO}_2(\text{s}) + \text{SO}_4^{2-}(\text{aq}) + 4\text{H}^+(\text{aq}) + 2\text{e}^- \rightarrow \text{PbSO}_4(\text{s}) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(\text{l})\)
C. Cathode reaction during discharge of lead storage batteryIII. \(\text{Zn(Hg)} + 2\text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{ZnO}(\text{s}) + \text{H}_2\text{O} + 2\text{e}^-\)
D. Cathodic reaction during atmospheric rusting of ironIV. \(\text{MnO}_2 + \text{NH}_4^+ + \text{e}^- \rightarrow \text{MnO(OH)} + \text{NH}_3\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Identification of Electrode Half-Reactions
Specific reduction and oxidation processes take place at designated electrode surfaces in batteries and corrosion cells.

Step 2: Reaction Breakdown for Each System
At the cathode of a dry cell, manganese dioxide is reduced in the presence of ammonium ions: \(\text{MnO}_2 + \text{NH}_4^+ + \text{e}^- \rightarrow \text{MnO(OH)} + \text{NH}_3\), reducing manganese from \(+4\) to \(+3\).
At the anode of a mercury cell, zinc amalgam undergoes oxidation in the alkaline medium: \(\text{Zn(Hg)} + 2\text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{ZnO}(\text{s}) + \text{H}_2\text{O} + 2\text{e}^-\).
At the cathode of a lead storage battery during discharge, lead dioxide is reduced in acidic sulphate solution: \(\text{PbO}_2(\text{s}) + \text{SO}_4^{2-}(\text{aq}) + 4\text{H}^+(\text{aq}) + 2\text{e}^- \rightarrow \text{PbSO}_4(\text{s}) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(\text{l})\).
At the cathodic spot during the atmospheric rusting of iron, atmospheric oxygen dissolved in surface moisture is reduced by electrons arriving from anodic spots: \(\text{O}_2(\text{g}) + 4\text{H}^+(\text{aq}) + 4\text{e}^- \rightarrow 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(\text{l})\Defaultgrade.

Step 3: Pairwise Matching Evaluation
Cathode reaction in dry cell pairs with \(\text{MnO}_2 + \text{NH}_4^+ + \text{e}^- \rightarrow \text{MnO(OH)} + \text{NH}_3\).
Anode reaction in mercury cell pairs with \(\text{Zn(Hg)} + 2\text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{ZnO}(\text{s}) + \text{H}_2\text{O} + 2\text{e}^-\).
Cathode reaction in lead storage battery pairs with \(\text{PbO}_2(\text{s}) + \text{SO}_4^{2-}(\text{aq}) + 4\text{H}^+(\text{aq}) + 2\text{e}^- \rightarrow \text{PbSO}_4(\text{s}) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(\text{l})\).
Cathodic reaction during atmospheric rusting of iron pairs with \(\text{O}_2(\text{g}) + 4\text{H}^+(\text{aq}) + 4\text{e}^- \rightarrow 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(\text{l})\).

Step 4: Check and Final Conceptual Answer
The electron transfers, stoichiometry, and oxidation states match the authoritative chemical equations in Sections 2.6.1, 2.6.2, and 2.8.
Final Conceptual Answer: A pairs with IV, B pairs with III, C pairs with II, and D pairs with I.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MATCHING_MCQ_Q05 - Match electrolytic systems with electrolysis products

questiontext.text:
Match the electrolyte being electrolysed using inert platinum electrodes in List I with the major electrode products in List II:

List IList II
A. Molten \(\text{NaCl}\)I. \(\text{H}_2(\text{g})\) at cathode and \(\text{S}_2\text{O}_8^{2-}(\text{aq})\) at anode
B. Aqueous \(\text{NaCl}\)II. \(\text{Na}(\text{s})\) at cathode and \(\text{Cl}_2(\text{g})\) at anode
C. Dilute \(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\)III. \(\text{H}_2(\text{g})\) at cathode and \(\text{Cl}_2(\text{g})\) at anode
D. Concentrated \(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\)IV. \(\text{H}_2(\text{g})\) at cathode and \(\text{O}_2(\text{g})\) at anode

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Principles of Electrolysis and Competing Electrode Reactions
At the cathode, the cation or species with the higher reduction potential discharges first. At the anode, the anion or species with the lower oxidation potential discharges preferentially unless overpotential effects dictate otherwise.

Step 2: Analysis of Each Electrolyte
In molten \(\text{NaCl}\), only \(\text{Na}^+\) and \(\text{Cl}^-\) ions are present. \(\text{Na}^+\) is reduced to \(\text{Na}(\text{s})\) at the cathode, and \(\text{Cl}^-\) is oxidised to \(\text{Cl}_2(\text{g})\) at the anode.
In aqueous \(\text{NaCl}\), reduction of water to \(\text{H}_2(\text{g})\) occurs at the cathode because its reduction potential is substantially higher than that of \(\text{Na}^+\) (\(-2.71\text{ V}\)). At the anode, although oxidation of water to \(\text{O}_2\) has a slightly lower standard potential (\(1.23\text{ V}\) versus \(1.36\text{ V}\) for chloride), the kinetic overpotential of oxygen makes chloride oxidation faster, producing \(\text{Cl}_2(\text{g})\).
In dilute \(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\), \(\text{H}^+\) is reduced to \(\text{H}_2(\text{g})\) at the cathode, and water is oxidised to \(\text{O}_2(\text{g})\) at the anode (\(E^\circ = 1.23\text{ V}\)).
In concentrated \(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\), the high concentration of sulphate ions favors oxidation to peroxodisulphate at the anode: \(2\text{SO}_4^{2-} \rightarrow \text{S}_2\text{O}_8^{2-} + 2\text{e}^-\) (\(E^\circ = 1.96\text{ V}\)), with \(\text{H}_2(\text{g})\) liberating at the cathode.

Step 3: Pairwise Matching Evaluation
Molten \(\text{NaCl}\) produces \(\text{Na}(\text{s})\) at cathode and \(\text{Cl}_2(\text{g})\) at anode.
Aqueous \(\text{NaCl}\) produces \(\text{H}_2(\text{g})\) at cathode and \(\text{Cl}_2(\text{g})\) at anode.
Dilute \(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\) produces \(\text{H}_2(\text{g})\) at cathode and \(\text{O}_2(\text{g})\) at anode.
Concentrated \(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\) produces \(\text{H}_2(\text{g})\) at cathode and \(\text{S}_2\text{O}_8^{2-}(\text{aq})\) at anode.

Step 4: Check and Final Conceptual Answer
Thermodynamic potentials and kinetic overpotentials corroborate each electrode assignment.
Final Conceptual Answer: A pairs with II, B pairs with III, C pairs with IV, and D pairs with I.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MATCHING_MCQ_Q06 - Match ionic species with limiting molar conductivities

questiontext.text:
Using the limiting molar ionic conductivities at \(298\text{ K}\) (\(\lambda^\circ\) in \(\text{S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\): \(\text{Ca}^{2+} = 119.0\), \(\text{Mg}^{2+} = 106.0\), \(\text{Cl}^- = 76.3\), \(\text{SO}_4^{2-} = 160.0\), \(\text{Na}^+ = 50.1\), \(\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^- = 40.9\)), match the electrolyte in List I with its limiting molar conductivity \(\Lambda_m^\circ\) (in \(\text{S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\)) in List II:

List IList II
A. \(\text{CaCl}_2\)I. \(126.4\)
B. \(\text{MgSO}_4\)II. \(266.0\)
C. \(\text{CH}_3\text{COONa}\)III. \(271.6\)
D. \(\text{NaCl}\)IV. \(91.0\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Relevant Principle (Kohlrausch Law)
Kohlrausch's law of independent migration of ions states that the limiting molar conductivity of an electrolyte equals the sum of the individual contributions of its constituent ions: \(\Lambda_m^\circ = \nu_+ \lambda_+^\circ + \nu_- \lambda_-^\circ\).

Step 2: Step-by-Step Numerical Additions
For \(\text{CaCl}_2\):
\(\Lambda_m^\circ(\text{CaCl}_2) = \lambda^\circ(\text{Ca}^{2+}) + 2\lambda^\circ(\text{Cl}^-) = 119.0 + 2(76.3) = 119.0 + 152.6 = 271.6\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\).
For \(\text{MgSO}_4\):
\(\Lambda_m^\circ(\text{MgSO}_4) = \lambda^\circ(\text{Mg}^{2+}) + \lambda^\circ(\text{SO}_4^{2-}) = 106.0 + 160.0 = 266.0\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\).
For \(\text{CH}_3\text{COONa}\):
\(\Lambda_m^\circ(\text{CH}_3\text{COONa}) = \lambda^\circ(\text{Na}^+) + \lambda^\circ(\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-) = 50.1 + 40.9 = 91.0\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\).
For \(\text{NaCl}\):
\(\Lambda_m^\circ(\text{NaCl}) = \lambda^\circ(\text{Na}^+) + \lambda^\circ(\text{Cl}^-) = 50.1 + 76.3 = 126.4\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\).

Step 3: Pairwise Matching Evaluation
\(\text{CaCl}_2\) yields \(271.6\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\).
\(\text{MgSO}_4\) yields \(266.0\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\).
\(\text{CH}_3\text{COONa}\) yields \(91.0\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\).
\(\text{NaCl}\) yields \(126.4\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\).

Step 4: Check and Final Conceptual Answer
Stoichiometric coefficients are appropriately applied for the divalent and univalent electrolytes.
Final Conceptual Answer: A pairs with III, B pairs with II, C pairs with IV, and D pairs with I.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MATCHING_MCQ_Q07 - Match redox couples with standard electrode potentials

questiontext.text:
Match the redox couples in List I with their standard reduction potentials \(E^\circ\) at \(298\text{ K}\) in List II:

List IList II
A. \(\text{F}_2(\text{g}) / \text{F}^-\)I. \(-0.76\text{ V}\)
B. \(\text{Cu}^{2+} / \text{Cu(s)}\)II. \(+2.87\text{ V}\)
C. \(\text{Zn}^{2+} / \text{Zn(s)}\)III. \(-3.05\text{ V}\)
D. \(\text{Li}^+ / \text{Li(s)}\)IV. \(+0.34\text{ V}\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Concept of Electrochemical Series
The standard reduction potential measures the thermodynamic tendency of a chemical species to accept electrons relative to the standard hydrogen electrode, which is set to \(0.00\text{ V}\).

Step 2: Detailed Values from the Standard Reduction Table
Fluorine exhibits the highest standard electrode potential in the electrochemical table, with \(E^\circ(\text{F}_2 / \text{F}^-) = +2.87\text{ V}\), indicating that fluorine gas is the strongest oxidising agent.
The copper couple has a positive potential: \(E^\circ(\text{Cu}^{2+} / \text{Cu}) = +0.34\text{ V}\).
The zinc couple has a negative potential: \(E^\circ(\text{Zn}^{2+} / \text{Zn}) = -0.76\text{ V}\).
Lithium has the lowest standard potential: \(E^\circ(\text{Li}^+ / \text{Li}) = -3.05\text{ V}\), which establishes lithium metal as the most powerful reducing agent in aqueous solution.

Step 3: Pairwise Matching Evaluation
\(\text{F}_2(\text{g}) / \text{F}^-\) corresponds to \(+2.87\text{ V}\).
\(\text{Cu}^{2+} / \text{Cu(s)}\) corresponds to \(+0.34\text{ V}\).
\(\text{Zn}^{2+} / \text{Zn(s)}\) corresponds to \(-0.76\text{ V}\).
\(\text{Li}^+ / \text{Li(s)}\) corresponds to \(-3.05\text{ V}\).

Step 4: Check and Final Conceptual Answer
The potential values match those tabulated in textbook standard reduction potential series at \(298\text{ K}\).
Final Conceptual Answer: A pairs with II, B pairs with IV, C pairs with I, and D pairs with III.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MATCHING_MCQ_Q08 - Match electrochemical conversions with charge required

questiontext.text:
Match the electrochemical conversion in List I with the theoretical quantity of electrical charge required in List II (using \(1\text{ F} \approx 96500\text{ C}\)):

List IList II
A. Reduction of \(1\text{ mol}\) of \(\text{Al}^{3+}\) to \(\text{Al}\)I. \(1\text{ F}\) (\(96500\text{ C}\))
B. Oxidation of \(1\text{ mol}\) of \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\) to \(\text{O}_2\)II. \(5\text{ F}\) (\(482500\text{ C}\))
C. Reduction of \(1\text{ mol}\) of \(\text{MnO}_4^-\) to \(\text{Mn}^{2+}\)III. \(2\text{ F}\) (\(193000\text{ C}\))
D. Oxidation of \(1\text{ mol}\) of \(\text{FeO}\) to \(\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3\)IV. \(3\text{ F}\) (\(289500\text{ C}\))

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Relevant Principle (Faraday's Laws of Electrolysis)
The total charge required to carry out an electrochemical transformation is determined by the reaction stoichiometry: \(Q = n F\), where \(n\) is the number of moles of electrons transferred per mole of substance.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Stoichiometric Calculations
For the reduction of \(\text{Al}^{3+}\) to \(\text{Al}\):
The cathode reaction is \(\text{Al}^{3+} + 3\text{e}^- \rightarrow \text{Al}\).
Reduction of \(1\text{ mol}\) of \(\text{Al}^{3+}\) requires \(3\text{ mol}\) of electrons: \(Q = 3\text{ F} = 3 \times 96500\text{ C} = 289500\text{ C}\).
For the oxidation of \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\) to \(\text{O}_2\):
The balanced half-reaction is \(2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{O}_2 + 4\text{H}^+ + 4\text{e}^-\).
Normalising for \(1\text{ mol}\) of \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\): \(\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \frac{1}{2}\text{O}_2 + 2\text{H}^+ + 2\text{e}^-\).
Thus, \(1\text{ mol}\) of \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\) releases \(2\text{ mol}\) of electrons: \(Q = 2\text{ F} = 2 \times 96500\text{ C} = 193000\text{ C}\).
For the reduction of \(\text{MnO}_4^-\) to \(\text{Mn}^{2+}\) in acidic solution:
The reaction is \(\text{MnO}_4^- + 8\text{H}^+ + 5\text{e}^- \rightarrow \text{Mn}^{2+} + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}\).
Manganese undergoes a change in oxidation state from \(+7\) to \(+2\), requiring \(5\text{ mol}\) of electrons: \(Q = 5\text{ F} = 5 \times 96500\text{ C} = 482500\text{ C}\).
For the oxidation of \(\text{FeO}\) to \(\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3\):
In \(\text{FeO}\), iron has oxidation state \(+2\), while in \(\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3\), iron has oxidation state \(+3\).
The half-reaction per mole of iron(II) is \(\text{Fe}^{2+} \rightarrow \text{Fe}^{3+} + \text{e}^-\).
Therefore, \(1\text{ mol}\) of \(\text{FeO}\) releases \(1\text{ mol}\) of electrons: \(Q = 1\text{ F} = 96500\text{ C}\).

Step 3: Pairwise Matching Evaluation
Reduction of \(1\text{ mol}\) of \(\text{Al}^{3+}\) requires \(3\text{ F}\) (\(289500\text{ C}\)).
Oxidation of \(1\text{ mol}\) of \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\) requires \(2\text{ F}\) (\(193000\text{ C}\)).
Reduction of \(1\text{ mol}\) of \(\text{MnO}_4^-\) requires \(5\text{ F}\) (\(482500\text{ C}\)).
Oxidation of \(1\text{ mol}\) of \(\text{FeO}\) requires \(1\text{ F}\) (\(96500\text{ C}\)).

Step 4: Check and Final Conceptual Answer
The values correspond to textbook Exercises 2.12 and 2.14.
Final Conceptual Answer: A pairs with IV, B pairs with III, C pairs with II, and D pairs with I.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MATCHING_MCQ_Q09 - Match electrolytic relations with functional forms

questiontext.text:
Match the electrochemical formula or parameter in List I with its mathematically equivalent expression in List II:

List IList II
A. Cell constant (\(G^*\))I. \(\frac{c\Lambda_m^2}{\Lambda_m^\circ(\Lambda_m^\circ - \Lambda_m)}\)
B. Molar conductivity (\(\Lambda_m\)) in terms of \(\kappa\) and molarity \(c\) (where \(\kappa\) is in \(\text{S cm}^{-1}\) and \(c\) in \(\text{mol L}^{-1}\))II. \(\Lambda_m^\circ - A c^{1/2}\)
C. Debye-Hückel-Onsager equation for strong electrolyteIII. \(\frac{\kappa \times 1000}{c}\)
D. Dissociation constant (\(K_a\)) of weak monobasic acid via Ostwald's dilution lawIV. \(R \cdot \kappa\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Relevant Electrochemical Equations
Electrolyte conductometry relies on specific mathematical formulations for geometric cell factors, unit conversions, empirical concentration dependencies, and weak electrolyte ionization equilibria.

Step 2: Detailed Algebraic Derivations
The cell constant is defined as \(G^* = \frac{l}{A}\). Because resistance is \(R = \frac{1}{\kappa}\frac{l}{A} = \frac{G^*}{\kappa}\), multiplying both sides by \(\kappa\) yields \(G^* = R \cdot \kappa\).
When conductivity \(\kappa\) is expressed in \(\text{S cm}^{-1}\) and concentration \(c\) in \(\text{mol L}^{-1}\), since \(1\text{ L} = 1000\text{ cm}^3\), the volume containing one mole of solute is \(V = \frac{1000}{c}\text{ cm}^3\text{ mol}^{-1}\). Hence, molar conductivity is given by \(\Lambda_m = \frac{\kappa \times 1000}{c}\) in \(\text{S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\).
For a strong electrolyte, the Debye-Hückel-Onsager relation expresses the decrease of molar conductivity with square root of concentration as \(\Lambda_m = \Lambda_m^\circ - A c^{1/2}\).
For a weak monobasic acid, the degree of dissociation is given by \(\alpha = \frac{\Lambda_m}{\Lambda_m^\circ}\). Substituting this into Ostwald's dilution law \(K_a = \frac{c \alpha^2}{1 - \alpha}\) gives:
\(K_a = \frac{c (\Lambda_m / \Lambda_m^\circ)^2}{1 - (\Lambda_m / \Lambda_m^\circ)} = \frac{c \Lambda_m^2}{(\Lambda_m^\circ)^2 \left(\frac{\Lambda_m^\circ - \Lambda_m}{\Lambda_m^\circ}\right)} = \frac{c \Lambda_m^2}{\Lambda_m^\circ(\Lambda_m^\circ - \Lambda_m)}\).

Step 3: Pairwise Matching Evaluation
Cell constant pairs with \(R \cdot \kappa\).
Molar conductivity in \(\text{S cm}^{-1}\) and \(\text{mol L}^{-1}\) pairs with \(\frac{\kappa \times 1000}{c}\).
Debye-Hückel-Onsager equation pairs with \(\Lambda_m^\circ - A c^{1/2}\).
Dissociation constant of weak monobasic acid pairs with \(\frac{c\Lambda_m^2}{\Lambda_m^\circ(\Lambda_m^\circ - \Lambda_m)}\).

Step 4: Check and Final Conceptual Answer
Every equation is rigorously confirmed against textbook Sections 2.4.1 and 2.4.2.
Final Conceptual Answer: A pairs with IV, B pairs with III, C pairs with II, and D pairs with I.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MATCHING_MCQ_Q10 - Match thermodynamic and electrochemical equilibrium relationships

questiontext.text:
Match the electrochemical thermodynamic parameter or quantity in List I with its computed value or analytical expression at \(298\text{ K}\) in List II:

List IList II
A. Standard Gibbs energy change (\(\Delta_r G^\circ\)) for Daniell cell (\(E_{\text{cell}}^\circ = 1.1\text{ V}\), \(n = 2\), \(F = 96487\text{ C mol}^{-1}\))I. \(-nFE_{\text{cell}}\)
B. Equilibrium constant formulation (\(\log K_c\)) from standard cell potentialII. \(1.10\text{ V} - \frac{0.059}{2}\text{ V} = 1.0705\text{ V}\)
C. Gibbs energy change (\(\Delta_r G\)) of reaction at non-standard stateIII. \(-212.27\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)
D. Cell potential (\(E_{\text{cell}}\)) of Daniell cell when \(\frac{[\text{Zn}^{2+}]}{[\text{Cu}^{2+}]} = 10\) at \(298\text{ K}\)IV. \(\frac{n E_{\text{cell}}^\circ}{0.059\text{ V}}\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Relevant Thermodynamic and Electrochemical Equations
Electrical work performed reversibly relates to Gibbs free energy change via \(\Delta_r G = -nFE_{\text{cell}}\) and \(\Delta_r G^\circ = -nFE_{\text{cell}}^\circ\). The equilibrium constant links to standard cell potential via \(E_{\text{cell}}^\circ = \frac{2.303RT}{nF}\log K_c = \frac{0.059\text{ V}}{n}\log K_c\) at \(298\text{ K}\), and concentration variations are given by the Nernst equation.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Numerical and Formulaic Evaluations
For the standard Daniell cell reaction \(\text{Zn(s)} + \text{Cu}^{2+}(\text{aq}) \rightarrow \text{Zn}^{2+}(\text{aq}) + \text{Cu(s)}\):
Here \(n = 2\), \(E_{\text{cell}}^\circ = 1.1\text{ V}\), and \(F = 96487\text{ C mol}^{-1}\).
\(\Delta_r G^\circ = -nFE_{\text{cell}}^\circ = -2 \times 96487\text{ C mol}^{-1} \times 1.1\text{ V} = -212271.4\text{ J mol}^{-1} = -212.27\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).
At equilibrium (\(E_{\text{cell}} = 0\)), \(E_{\text{cell}}^\circ = \frac{0.059\text{ V}}{n}\log K_c\).
Rearranging gives \(\log K_c = \frac{n E_{\text{cell}}^\circ}{0.059\text{ V}}\).
At non-standard conditions, the Gibbs free energy change is directly given by \(\Delta_r G = -nFE_{\text{cell}}\).
Applying the Nernst equation to the Daniell cell at \(298\text{ K}\):
\(E_{\text{cell}} = E_{\text{cell}}^\circ - \frac{0.059\text{ V}}{2}\log \frac{[\text{Zn}^{2+}]}{[\text{Cu}^{2+}]}\).
Substituting the concentration ratio \(\frac{[\text{Zn}^{2+}]}{[\text{Cu}^{2+}]} = 10\):
Since \(\log(10) = 1\), \(E_{\text{cell}} = 1.10\text{ V} - \frac{0.059}{2}\text{ V} = 1.10\text{ V} - 0.0295\text{ V} = 1.0705\text{ V}\).

Step 3: Pairwise Matching Evaluation
Standard Gibbs energy change for the Daniell cell corresponds to \(-212.27\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).
Equilibrium constant expression corresponds to \(\frac{n E_{\text{cell}}^\circ}{0.059\text{ V}}\).
Gibbs energy change of reaction corresponds to \(-nFE_{\text{cell}}\).
Cell potential of Daniell cell when ion concentration ratio is \(10\) corresponds to \(1.10\text{ V} - \frac{0.059}{2}\text{ V} = 1.0705\text{ V}\).

Step 4: Check and Final Conceptual Answer
All derived values agree with the calculations presented in textbook Examples 2.1, 2.3 and Section 2.3.2.
Final Conceptual Answer: A pairs with III, B pairs with IV, C pairs with I, and D pairs with II.
